utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Absent from the Defence teams I notice Mr. Bourgon, Mr. Lazarevic, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Krgovic, and Mr. Haynes. Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer who are present. Witness is already in the courtroom. So I suppose we can proceed. Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Nikolic. Yesterday during your testimony we dealt with the relationship between the brothers. However, I have one question left in that area. Were you mobilised between 1992 and 1996 to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak into the microphone to her right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, you need to either come nearer the microphone or use another microphone, the interpreters are not hearing you well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will endeavour to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it better, I'm asking the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In 1992 when the war broke out in Bosnia, what happened with Drago Nikolic's family?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago was in Sarajevo with his family. At the moment when the war broke out, he was in a barracks. He had already been mobilised. His wife was in the military hospital. He managed to transfer his children to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recall what was happening with the daughters of your brother in April 1992 after he had transferred them to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. Drago called me on the 6th of April, 1992, in the morning, to tell me that he transferred them to Pale, and that I should pick them up to take them to my house. I asked a neighbour of mine to accompany me to Pale. In the meantime, Drago called our elder brother Dragan that the children were to be picked up in Pale. Dragan did so and brought them to Kravica where he handed them over to me. Then I took them to my place in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How old were they at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragana was 13 and Vida 11.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Dragana and Vida, did they spend a period of time in Novi Sad with you and your family?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed until the end of July that year. After having been brought from Pale, I enrolled them in a school in their respective grades which they completed in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And that was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: While Drago's children were with you, how did Dragana and Vida take that situation being separated from the parents?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With difficulty. The younger girl, Vida, was crying a lot and whenever she would get back home from school, the first question she'd ask me was, Uncle, did daddy call? They suffered a lot and were very worried about their parents.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What about you and your wife, did you do your utmost in the circumstances that prevailed?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did everything trying to compensate for the fact that they missed their parents. We did not make a difference between them and our children. We even included them on school trips with the other children from the school so that they would feel a part of that community.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Between April and June 1992, when did Drago and his wife come to see the children, and did you know of their fate during those couple of months?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't hear anything about Drago until mid-June, for over two months, when he appeared in Novi Sad. His wife had arrived before that, around mid-May. As I said, Drago followed in mid-June.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Having left Sarajevo, do you know where your brother Drago Nikolic was sent to?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once he had left Sarajevo and spent a few days with me, he went back to Sekovici, that's where his next post was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know when it was that he was transferred to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Concerning their family circumstances, I wanted to ask you what was the relationship like between Drago and your wife, Ruza?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their relationship was a fair one. They respected each other. Drago held my wife in high esteem, and in the difficult -- the most difficult times, he entrusted her with his children. He particularly respected her for her good treatment of his children.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before he began his military studies, what was he like as a young man?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was of a merry spirit, well liked in his circle of friends and in the neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he change once he had completed his military studies?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he grew more serious, an introvert. It wasn't like it used to be before he went to the military school.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know what caused that change?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He often said that it was very difficult for him to be separated from the family during the four years being in the boarding school. He seldom visited home, only during national holidays. Their summer vacation was far shorter than that of civilian students.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would like to change topics now. In the course of the war between 1992 and 1995, did you go to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average, I went there once a month. Since my three brothers were there as well as my parents, I went there frequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, were you in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July 1995 I did go, in early July, to visit my brothers and parents, and there was something that I had to do there. I returned on the 9th of July since by that time the fighting around Srebrenica had started and I had my wife and children with me. Dragan also suggested that I should return and we went back to Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you see Drago Nikolic before going home that weekend?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While we were on our way back, we dropped by his barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When you were going to the barracks to see your own brother, what was the procedure like for you to be admitted inside the barracks where the Zvornik Brigade was quartered?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the reception desk there were military policeman, they asked for my ID, and then -- well, sometimes one of them would take us up to Drago's office or alternatively they would call him and then he would come down to see us.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since you were informed that the fighting had begun, once you returned to Novi Sad, were you interested in finding out what was happening with your brothers and with your brother in the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I frequently called, inquiring about Drago and even more about Boro, because a few days later, I think it was the 14th of July, from Boro's wife's father I learned that Boro was at Odrc that day, searching the terrain there.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recall an event that would be important for your family that may have taken place in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It was when our cousin Dusan Nikolic, on our uncle's side, was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: How did you learn of Dusan Nikolic being killed?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I called Drago's office to ask him if he knew where Boro was. Since he didn't respond, I called his house thinking that maybe he was at home for lunch. He picked up the phone there and told me that he didn't know where Boro was, but that he would let me know once he is back in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called in the afternoon. He was quite upset and said that Dusko had been killed. I asked him if he knew where Boro was, and he said he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can you recall what date that was?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. The 16th of July, the day when Dusko Nikolic was killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you at some point go to Zvornik in July 1995 after having learned this?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Drago told me about that, in the next half hour with a neighbour of mine, I set off towards Zvornik since I had no vehicle of mine. Once in Zvornik, I located my brother Borislav at the bridge in Karakaj. After that we went together to his home. Later on we went to Dusko's sister's apartment. Her name is Mara Milosevic. The family assembled there. We wanted to express our condolences. I found Drago there. There were many other family members there. They were making arrangements for the funeral that was to take place the next day. Drago took over the organisation of the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you attend Dusan Nikolic's funeral?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was this funeral, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the cortege headed out of Zvornik around noon and I think the funeral itself may have taken place at around 3 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you this: You've described the close relations that you had with Drago and the other brothers. Did Drago tell you about his service in the army, his job in Sarajevo and later on in Zvornik and Sekovici?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I tried to broach this subject several times with him, in particular when I was younger, but he always refused to discuss it. He would always tell me that there was no reason for me to know anything because this was all military secret.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you know any of Drago's colleagues, officers that he worked or socialized with in Sarajevo while he served in Sarajevo? What were his relations with those people?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew quite a few people in Sarajevo because I went there to visit him quite often. I know some of them by name, Lizdek, Matic, Milidrag. I knew quite a few of them by sight and, as far as I was able to observe, Drago was on good terms with all of them. They socialised, some of them would even come to our family home in Kravica. And when his child died all of them came to the funeral, regardless of their religion. All of those colleagues that I knew and those colleagues that I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the name, you said Matic and then Milidrag but it was wrongly recorded in the transcript?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Matic, Marinko, and Milidrag. Milidrag is the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if Drago was on good terms with his colleagues in Zvornik while he worked there?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know as a many of his colleagues from Zvornik. I knew them mostly from his stories. When I came to visit him I would see some of them in passing, but from what I heard from him and from what I heard from our brother Boro, he was on relatively good terms with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did he have any problems with any of those colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after he retired, he did mention at one point, he recounted that Obrenovic had contacted him -- I don't know what his rank was at the time -- insisting to see him. And when they did meet, he told Drago that he would drag Drago and the others into the pits. I don't know who the others were.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did Drago tell you why?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just the bare bones. He said that this man suspected Drago and others, other colleagues of having conspired against him. He didn't tell me any specifics, but at any rate, he suspected Drago of conspiring against him together with some other colleagues and that's why he threatened to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When was the first time that you heard that your brother had been indicted before the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the fall of 2002.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Where did Drago and his family live at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In their home in Banja Koviljaca, in their house.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you contact him at that time after the indictment was issued and were there any changes in his lifestyle?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I contacted -- I was in contact with Drago, I went to visit him and he would come to Novi Sad often to work. I found him different jobs then he would go back. So he continued his life as usual.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Drago's closest family had any problems after the indictment was issued?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that his wife and his daughter, his younger daughter were called -- were summoned to come to the police station in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Were you ever summoned to come to the police station or did anyone come to ask questions about Drago or questioned you and your family?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Nobody ever contacted me or asked me any questions. I continued to visit my parents quite frequently. I travelled to Bosnia, and when my ID was checked at the border, nobody asked me any questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to go back to an error in the transcript, that's page 8 line 21. My colleague has just pointed this out to me. At the very end of line 21 instead of the witness actually said he told Drago, not me. But I can explain that by asking some additional questions if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think it's clear enough. I don't think you need to, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss this indictment and the events with your brother, the events related to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we discussed it quite often in fact. He found it hard to bear. He would tell me that the things that are written in the indictment are not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So from October 2002 until March 2005, did you ever talk to Drago about his surrender to the International Criminal Tribunal in The Hague after this indictment was issued in 2002?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did talk to him about that a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was this campaign throughout the country in the media, on TV, in the press, that people should not surrender and he always used to say that officers higher in rank than he was had not surrendered yet. And he was also concerned about his family; his wife is quite ill. And at that time his children didn't hold steady jobs, so he was not ready to surrender yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What was your advice to him?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that he had to make this decision himself, but whatever he decided, I would be there -- I would support him, I would be at his side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did Drago decide to surrender to the ICTY at one point? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He called me in March 2005, early March, and he told me that he had to discuss something with me. He came to my place on the 12th of March and he said that he had decided to surrender, that he could no longer bear the pressure on his family. And he also saw that others were beginning to surrender. He wanted me to get in touch with somebody in the Serbian government to effect his surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you help him?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the 12th, I got in touch with some people in the government and we agreed that we should come on the 14th, that they would see us on the 14th. I, my wife and Drago went to Belgrade. We parked our car close to the Serbian government building. We went -- I went to the gate and some people came out and Drago accompanied them into the government building to negotiate his surrender. After a while they left, they came out and they said that they had agreed that he would leave for The Hague on the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of March?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of March.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, you described your family, the relationship between the brothers and in general the family relations. Could you tell us throughout these years, did Drago ever show any signs of ethnic or religious intolerance towards any family members or friends?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago never evinced any ethnic or religious intolerance. He was a Yugoslav, that was his orientation. He got on well with all people of all religions and ethnic backgrounds and his relationship with my wife is a good example of that. She is Catholic and also Drago's relationship with her parents. He often went to see them when he came to visit me. He would call them and to wish them happy for their feasts, religious feasts on so on and to this day he always asks me about how my wife is and how her parents are.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the end, Mr. Nikolic, I would like to ask you to answer just one more question. How would you describe your brother Drago's character and his relations with people in the community where the two of you grew up together?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my brother Drago was always a hard working man. He was well liked in his family but also in our broader community. He always wanted to assist everyone and he did, and people had a great deal of respect for that. And they showed their respect in particular now when the Trial Chamber allowed my brother to come to my father's wake, a 40-day wake. Lots of neighbours, lots of friends, family came in order to express their condolences to the family, but primarily to Drago because of his father's death and to pay their respects to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have no question for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, merci. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you and Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My name is Nelson Thayer. I'll be asking you some questions on behalf of the Prosecution. Now, you mentioned yesterday sir, and again today, that you were not mobilised into the VRS during the war. Can you tell the Trial Chamber how you performed your military service during the war, please?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not perform any military service. I went to Bosnia as a civilian. I'm a citizen of Serbia and that's where I lived, I only went there to visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the war, did you serve in the military of the Former Republic of Yugoslavia at the time, the FRY?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I did not serve in the military in the FRY either.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And did you have some work obligation or other reason why you did not serve in the military during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I worked in Novi Sad where I live, it's a normal job. It was not work obligation. I was paid for it. And I did my military service in 1983 and 1984.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And your eldest brother Dragan, how did he perform his military service during the war, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My brother Dragan was mobilised at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in what unit did he serve?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan was mobilised into the reserve force of the police, that was before the war. And when the war started, he was in a unit in Kravica where he remained until March 1993 when he lost his leg, and then he was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if I've done my math right, sir, your brother Dragan is the eldest, followed by your brother Drago, followed by yourself, and then followed by your late brother Borislav who was the youngest; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I think you mentioned yesterday that Borislav had a degree in mining. Did he attend the military academy?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did he have any police or law enforcement training, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my brother Borislav did his national service in 1984 and into 1985, and I don't recall what branch of service he was in. I know that he was in Nis, but I really don't know what branch he was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say, sir, that to your knowledge he didn't have, prior to the outbreak of the war in Bosnia, any specific police or law enforcement training?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what training he underwent in the military, but I don't think that he underwent any other kind of training outside of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did your brother Drago ever help your youngest brother Borislav at all or use any connections he may have had to help Borislav become a member of the Zvornik Brigade Military Police Company as opposed to remaining a foot soldier or conscript on the frontlines?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if it helped or not, but I do know that I had quarrels with Drago several times because I criticized him for not preventing Borislav going to various frontlines where the fighting was quite fierce. I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, are you aware of any times when or occasions when your brother Drago tried or succeeded in intervening on Borislav's behalf to keep him out of harm's way?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my previous answer I said that Drago went to the frontlines where there was fighting, and that I criticized Drago for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My question, sir, was: Did your brother Drago ever attempt to intervene, did he ever try or succeed in intervening on Borislav's behalf to keep him out of harm's way during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this is asked and answered twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't think it has been answered. He simply said that they had disagreements and I'm asking a specific question, did he try and did he ever succeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed with your answer. Let's proceed with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, never. He never helped him in any way or at least I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are certainly aware that in July 1995 hundreds and hundreds of Muslim men and boys from Srebrenica were detained at the Grbavci School in Orahovac and then executed nearby; right?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Is it your testimony, sir, that you've never heard that that occurred?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. There were all kinds of reports in the media, on TV, in the press. I'm just saying that I personally have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, we have information that, and this is from members of the Zvornik Brigade Military Police Company, that your brothers Drago and Borislav were both at that school in Orahovac on that day that the executions occurred?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Do you speak English? Do you understand English, Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not even a little bit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Can you remove your headphones, please. Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, [In English] Sorry, I can address you only in English. I will try to do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that this witness very clearly said that he was not mobilised, that he was not the citizen of Bosnia Herzegovina, that he was not in the war in Bosnia, that he is not living in Bosnia, and that he know nothing about the events. Everything what he heard, he heard from media. [Interpretation] I think this question is inappropriate [In English] Sorry, because I think that the question is completely inappropriate because that witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, I got your point -- we got your point. Mr. Thayer, do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Ever so briefly, Mr. President. We've heard from this witness that he discussed the indictment with Mr. Nikolic, that he was in touch with Mr. Nikolic following the attack on the Srebrenica enclave, that he has very specific recollection of certain dates in mid-July 1995. And I think I'm perfectly entitled to explore these issues and specific issues surrounding what happened in Orahovac to test this witness's memory and his credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic, and that's the end of it. In English, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Orahovac was never mentioned in my direct examination. An indictment meaning like the counts or text or charges were never part of my direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we come to the conclusion that your objection cannot be sustained, Ms. Nikolic, because not having been part of the war himself or part of the forces, VRS, not having firsthand information of what happened in Orahovac until he came to know through the media perhaps has got nothing to do with other information, the other information that is being solicited or he is being asked upon now by Mr. Thayer. So, Mr. Nikolic. You had started your question, you did not conclude it, in my opinion. I may be wrong. Go to page 16, lines 20 to 23, Mr. Thayer, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We are getting there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll just pick up right from there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, we have information from two military policemen from the Zvornik Brigade Military Police Company, Goran Bogdanovic and Cedo Jovic, that on the day that the executions at Orahovac occurred, your brother Drago's driver arrived at the school after the prisoners had all been placed inside the gym, summoned your youngest brother Borislav to the car and drove him away. Mr. Bogdanovic was very specific about that recollection and Mr. Jovic said the following about that. He said that: "This was a sufficient signal that even before anything had happened, we should allow ourselves, even if that included taking some risks, because of potential later responsibility, that we should just run away from the spot." And they did indeed flee according to their statements to us. Now, you testified that as brothers you helped each other out, growing up, throughout your entire lives. Did either of your brothers Drago or Borislav tell you about Drago sending his driver to the Orahovac school to take Borislav out of that place?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did your brother Drago ever tell you he was there at the school on the 13th or 14th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I have already stated that neither in peacetime nor in wartime he ever shared any such things with me. He never talked about that to me and I have no answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I understand that on occasions when you asked him about what his duties were and what his activities were, he replied that it was a military secret, sir. But I'm talking about what I don't think can be denied was a very, very widely reported massacre. And you've told us that you discussed the indictment with your brother Drago, and that he said that the things that were included in it weren't true. So I'm going to ask you some questions about some of these events, sir, and see whether you talked about some of these specific things. Did he ever tell you that he was angry about what happened at Orahovac, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never read the indictment. I have never discussed the details of the indictment with him. He has never mentioned any of those details.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the story about a little Muslim boy who was wounded during the mass execution at Orahovac and take to the Zvornik hospital? Surely your brother would have told you how outraged he was about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Avoid putting questions this way, Mr. Thayer, please. The first part of your question would have sufficed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were different stories in the media, in the press, on TV. I don't remember that particular story about that boy. In any case, I did not hear about it from Drago. For years people have been writing about such things. I may have read something of the sort along the way, but I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, will you allow that the Drago Nikolic who you know when he is with your family and behaved in a certain way when he was with your family may have behaved differently while he was performing his duties in the army during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very clear about the thrust of your question. I know my brother is a fair, honest person --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can move to the next question. He wasn't with him when he was at work both before, during and after the war. I mean, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: My last question for you, sir, is at any time before, during or, well, certainly after the war, did your brother express to you any sorrow, any sympathy, any remorse for the thousands and thousands of men and boys from Srebrenica who were executed in his area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: MILISAV NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, we have never discussed such matters. I can't tell you whether he demonstrated anything of the sort when we didn't discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, your testimony ends here. You will receive assistance from our staff to facilitate your return back home. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having come over to give evidence and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, exhibits? You used a couple in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think the list was distributed and it has two documents on it, the two we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Thayer?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it the other Defence teams are not interested so the two documents are admitted. You don't have any document, Mr. Thayer, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: None, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Let's move to the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, madam.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm the Presiding Judge. I wish to welcome you. I know this is not a nice occasion for you, but the Defence team of your father has summoned you to give evidence and accordingly before you start your testimony you are required to make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the whole truth. Madam Usher who is standing next to you is going to give you the text. Please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Make yourself comfortable, please. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Before we introduce ourselves, I would kindly ask you that you speak up so that the interpreters will be able to hear when you speak, and to pause between questions and answers so that there will be no overlaps and to have a clear transcript.

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wanted to introduce myself. My name is Ms. Nikolic, and I appear on behalf of your father, Drago Nikolic. Can you tell us your first and last name and your maiden name.

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: My name is Vida Vasic. Maiden name Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When and where were you born?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 3rd of October, 1980, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You are Drago Nikolic's daughter, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, Drago Nikolic is my father.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: I am a salesperson.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your educational background, what degrees do you hold?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: I have a junior college diploma as -- what we call it is an economics technician in the field of economic affairs.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember having given a statement on the 23rd of April, 2008, to Mr. Drago Nikolic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to revisit your statement in the few days prior to your testimony here?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I reread it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to Rule 92 ter I would like to read out this witness's statement, summary statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness lives in Mali Zvornik, Serbia. Drago Nikolic is her father. She has one sister Dragana and they also had a younger brother Dragisa, who died in 1990 as a result of serious illness when he was eight years old. The witness remembers that after the war broke out in Sarajevo in April 1992, Drago Nikolic took her and her sister to Pale where they spent three days. Afterwards, the brother of Drago Nikolic arrived and took them to Novi Sad to their uncle Milisav Nikolic. Drago and Milena Nikolic remained in Sarajevo. The witness and her sister stayed in Novi Sad for two to three months where they completed that school year. Mother Milena joined them a month later. After that, they saw Drago Nikolic again in June 1992. In the summer of 1992, they moved to Sekovici and then to Zvornik where they stayed until the end of the war. In July 1995 they lived in Zvornik. The witness remembers the 16th of July, 1995, when their uncle Dusan Nikolic was killed. The witness remembers that day since besides her uncle being killed, her mother Milena's birthday is on that day too. At the time of family birthdays and get-togethers, they always tried to be together as a family. The witness remembers that on that day Drago Nikolic came home to attend a family lunch since it was his [as interpreted] mother's birthday. The witness does not remember the exact time but, according to the best of her recollection, she thinks that Drago stayed in the house until mid-afternoon. On the 16th of July, 1995, they were informed at home that Dusan Nikolic was killed. The whole family was shaken since Drago Nikolic and Dusan were very close. The witness remembers that it was in the afternoon when Mara Milosevic, Dusan Nikolic's sister, called and asked to speak to Drago Nikolic. Mara called because she wanted to know about Dusan, however, Drago Nikolic had already left the house. The witness had already known that Dusan Nikolic had been killed by that time but neither she nor her mother wanted to tell that to Mara. The witness remembers that her father played a significant role during the funeral and that he left the next day after Dusan had been killed. This concludes my reading of the summary according to Rule 92 ter, and I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic, if I just interrupt you for a moment. If you look at the transcript at page 24, line 22, it says: "To attend a family lunch since it was his mother's birthday," that's different from what is in the same where she indicates it was her mother's birthday. So I think that needs to be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will repeat my question for the sake of the transcript. It was indeed her mother.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Was that your mother's birthday?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, my mother's birthday.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The summary of statement I read out, does it reflect truly and accurately the statement you gave to our Defence team?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are the facts you mentioned in your statement true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do they truly reflect the facts that you would repeat before this Tribunal if asked the same questions today?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this point, Your Honour, I seek to tender Vida Vasic's statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. We'll come to that later. I would take it there's no objection? So you can assume that it is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. It is 3D474. I have only a few questions for Mrs. Vasic, but since there are only a couple of minutes left before the break, this may be a good time to take that break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Nikolic, we'll have a 25-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasic, you spent about two months in the house of your uncle and aunt. Do you remember when your parents joined you in Novi Sad in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. My mother, Milena, joined us first and then a month later -- that was about a month after we left, and my father joined us about two months later.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have any news from your parents in the intervening period?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any news of my parents. They remained in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And how did you bear those days when you were separated from your family?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: Well, this was a difficult period for me since my sister and I were very close and devoted to our parents. I went to school and although the school recognised our previous grades, I would always come home from school every day and I would ask my Uncle Milisav if there had been any news and if my parents had left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasic, how would you describe the relations in your family and Drago Nikolic as your father?

utterances.speaker: VIDA VASIC
utterances.text: I am very proud of the fact that Drago Nikolic is my father. I'm very proud of all the love and all the support that he has given me. He has been a wonderful father. He never raised his voice in our house, neither at me or at my sister. We've always been able to deal with everything by talking about it. We spent a lot of time talking to each other. All his free time he devoted to us. He took care of us. He took care of our education. Although me and my sister Dragana were A students, whenever there was any need to help us with our school work, he would always be there for us. He always helped us. He attended all parent/teacher conferences. He really took our education to heart, and he spent all his free time with us. He took us out for walks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Vasic, if you find this difficult, we can stop now.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I take it I don't need to make the roll call, I would imagine no one is interested except maybe Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And Mrs. Vasic, I don't have any questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and neither have we, I suppose, which means, Mrs. Vasic, that your testimony comes to an end here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I wish to thank you for having been kind enough to come over and give testimony in this case. And on behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it there are no exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Except for the statement, of course, which I already said is --

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, but it's already been admitted, if I understand it correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. All right. Your next witness is Milosevic, isn't it? Dragan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is also a 92 ter witness, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, to you, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence as a Defence witness for Drago Nikolic. Before you do so, you are required by our rules to make a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. Text is being handed to you now, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We've met before?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: But could you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 10th of December, 1951, in the village of Jalovik, Vladimirci municipality in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What degrees do you hold and what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I completed the secondary teachers school in Sabac and I currently in the elementary school in Zvornik as a teacher.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During the war in Bosnia between 1992 and 1995, were you mobilised into the units of the Republika Srpska Army, when and for how long if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do recall. I was mobilised several times. The overall duration was about five months. I was mobilised right at the beginning, on the 20th of May, and that was until the 3rd of August, 1992. And then I was again mobilised twice in 1995, from the 27th of March until the 29th of April, and then again from the 15th of July until the end of August, the 30th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, one question, what is your current occupation, could you explain that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I teach in the elementary school Sveti Sava in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: When were you demobilised?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was demobilised on the 30th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you gave a statement to Drago Nikolic's Defence team on the 23rd of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have an occasion to read your statement before you signed it and again, in the couple of days before you took the stand?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I did have an opportunity to read it and I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the Rule 92 ter, I will now, Your Honours, read a brief summary of this statement. The witness lives in Zvornik and he is a teacher at the elementary school in Zvornik. The witness's wife is Mara Milosevic who is the sister of the late Dusan Nikolic and a cousin of Drago Nikolic. During the war, the witness had the work obligation as school teacher in the elementary school Sveti Sava in Zvornik. He was mobilised to the reserve battalion of the Zvornik Brigade and he remembers that he spent the night between the 15th and the 16th of July, 1995, in the Standard barracks. On the 16th of July, 1995, early in the afternoon, the witness was at the cemetery in Zvornik as a member of the honour guard firing blanks for a soldier who had been killed, and then there he learned from Drago Gajic that his relative Dusan Nikolic had been killed. The witness remembers that between 3 and 4 p.m. he went to the command in Standard where he found Drago Nikolic who was deeply upset. Dusan and Drago were inseparable from their childhood until Dusan's death. The witness went, together with Drago Nikolic and Mico Petkovic, to tell his wife Mara about this tragic event. On the 16th of July, 1995, starting from the afternoon all the way until the 17th of July, 1995, late in the evening, Drago Nikolic was with them at all times and he handled the complete funeral organisation of the late Dusan Nikolic who was buried in the Kravica cemetery on the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This concludes my 92 ter summary of your statement. Now, I would like to ask you whether what I have just read reflects the statement that you gave to the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in full.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The facts contained in the statement, are they true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They are completely true.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And do they reflect accurately your -- what you would say in front of this Trial Chamber if you were asked to testify about those events?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this time I would like that the witness statement provided this witness, 3D475, be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection? No objection from anyone. It is admitted, Ms. Nikolic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, now I would like to ask you just a couple of questions. How long have you known Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, from the time when I came to my job in Kravica, that's in 1973 [Realtime transcript read in error "1993"] in the Petar Kocic elementary school, I lived in the immediate vicinity of Drago Nikolic's family house, so I've known him since 1973 when he was my student.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And when did you get to know him better?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I got to know Drago better in 1977 when I married his relative Mara Nikolic, and we socialised to a greater extent from 1993 when he came to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I would just like to correct for the record that page 32, line 18, could you please repeat the year, the first time that you heard about Drago Nikolic when you got the job in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was 1973.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Not 1993, then?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Since you've known Drago Nikolic and his family for over 30 years based on your answers, could you please describe to us what kind of a person Drago Nikolic was as a man? What would you say about his family and his character?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've known Drago Nikolic since his early youth, since he was 16. I could tell you a lot of things about him, but as a member of his wider family, I can tell you that he was a respected -- well respected. Even when he was young, when he was a student, his family respected him and he was always ready to assist anyone in any situation, anyone in his closer or broader family. There was a tragedy in his family and it affected him deeply, he lost his son. And after that, his hair went completely white. It was really a striking thing that happened for all of us. I was there with them. And in 1993, since that time, he socialised -- socialised with us with our family because the late Dusan lived with us in our apartment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Mr. Milosevic. Thank you, Your Honours. I don't have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any one of the Defence teams interested in cross-examining this witness. None. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: A few, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. My name is Peter McCloskey, I represent the Prosecution in this case. Can you tell me where you were living in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995 I lived in Zvornik, in Brace Jugovica Street B7, apartment number 15, and that's where I reside nowadays as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you have family living in the Kravica area in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, in Kravica, my wife's brothers lived there as well as her uncles. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let me just clarify a little something in your statement. You say you were in that honour guard on the 16th of July at the cemetery in Zvornik for a soldier Rajko Smiljanic -- sorry about the pronunciation. So were you able to confirm those dates for this statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that vividly. I was mobilised late in the afternoon on the 15th. There was a storm in Zvornik. After that, I was a member of the battalion in charge of the honourary guard at the Karakaj cemetery, because at that time there were supposed to be two funerals. I remember well Rajko Smiljanic since he was a manager's son. I knew the manager, having worked in the place where he used to work, and I remember that situation well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you are sure that the ceremony was on the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm completely certain of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And your statement says that immediately after that, meaning I think the ceremony, between 3 and 4 p.m. you say: "I went to the command in Standard and there I found Drago Nikolic." And so when you say that in your report, you mean immediately after the ceremony at the cemetery, you went to the Standard barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And why did you go to the barracks at Standard?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After the blanks were fired for Rajko Smiljanic, we talked to his father, waiting for the other funeral procession. I don't remember whose funeral it was exactly. In the meantime, a soldier arrived who was with the Zvornik command and told me the tragic news of Dusan Nikolic being killed. I was also allowed to leave and told that someone else would take over. I was told to report at Standard, so that the news of Dusan's tragic death could be conveyed to the rest of the family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do I understand you were allowed to go to Standard in order to tell Drago Nikolic about the tragic news?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was told to go to Standard and at Standard I came across Drago Nikolic who by that time had already known about the situation, and together with him and Milos Petkovic, aka Mica, I went to Zvornik to tell the news to my wife, his sister and his wife Dusica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know how long Drago Nikolic had known of the news about this tragedy before you had actually seen him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know then and I don't know now at what point he learned of that. I only knew that there were conflicts at Baljkovica and there were some people killed at the moment I left for the cemetery. As for Drago, I have no idea when he learned of the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And about what time did you see Drago at the Standard barracks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to know what time it was exactly, but I think between 3 and 4 in the afternoon, give or take half an hour. It's very difficult to pinpoint it exactly 13 years later, but it was sometime in the afternoon, maybe after 4 o'clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what part of the Standard barracks did you see him in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the entrance. Well, how should I explain it? As I was leaving the cemetery, since it is relatively close, when I arrived there, Mica Petkovic and Drago were already there, and we left together. So just close to the reception office at the gate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Outside the building or inside the building?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Outside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you remember if Drago Nikolic was in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was in uniform?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did Drago Nikolic live at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think at the time he lived in Zvornik. I don't know what the address was. I think it is an apartment block called Z14 or 15. That's the numbers that the buildings bear. In any case, it is in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to give us an idea, normal traffic driving from the Standard barracks to the apartment block, how long would it take? Just roughly.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you mean on foot or by car?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, let's start with car.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Up to five minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think that will be close enough. And do you know, was there a telephone in Drago Nikolic's house at that time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did Drago Nikolic have a Motorola with him some of the times when you would see him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. I don't remember whether he had it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And it's the next day, the 17th, that you went to the funeral in Kravica; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th in the evening, the family got together in my apartment because Dusan was living with us for awhile and then later he was given an apartment in Zvornik. In the afternoon, Dusan was taken from the morgue to his new apartment which was just above the pharmacy. The funeral took place in the afternoon on the 16th in Kravica. I know that the procession left the apartment around noon in the direction of Kravica and we couldn't go via Konjevic Polje. We had to take another route via Zelinje, Polonje [phoen] towards Bratunac and then on to Kravica, which was the late birth place of the late Dusan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help you clarify some of the dates. Sometimes we have translation errors, sometimes you may have mixed up the dates. I'll let you sort that out.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. The 16th in the evening is what I was talking about. I was mobilised on the 15th. On the 16th, I stood the honour guard and learned of Dusan's death. On the 16th, the family got together, and the 17th is when the funeral was in Kravica. Thank you for having corrected me. I did mix up the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: About what time did you leave from Zvornik to go to the funeral on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The procession set out from Zvornik, as far as I can remember, around noon. Was it quarter to 12 or 12 exactly, in any case around that time it set out, following the route I described, via Drinjaca, Zeljine, Polom to Bratunac, and then to the village cemetery in Bacacica [phoen] -- outside Kravica where the late Dusan Nikolic was buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That route you said you took, was that more of a gravel type road closer to the Drina to get to Bratunac to avoid that main road through Konjevic Polje?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That road was a dirt road from Zeljine to Bratunac. It was a gravel road and indeed we did not go by Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What time roughly did you, yourself, come back from the funeral in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was a member of the R Battalion, I returned late in the evening to Zvornik. The next day I reported to my unit. I came back to Zvornik on 17th in the evening. My wife and some of the family remained with their brothers in Bratunac since one of the brothers of the late Dusan at the time ran a bar in Bratunac where the religious ceremony took place after Dusan had been buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what time did the funeral end in Kravica on the 17th? And the ceremonies related to it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, since the religious ceremony was in the church in Bratunac, the procession went in the direction of Kravica to Dusan's native village. I think it was in late afternoon. A lot of time has passed. I can't tell you exactly what time it was. In any case, quite some time elapsed. We took the gravel road from Zvornik -- well, perhaps I could give you an estimate but nothing exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did you get back to Zvornik before dark the day of the funeral ceremony?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. As I said, I returned to Zvornik late in the evening so that I would be able to report back to the unit the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when you were on duty in the R Battalion, who was your brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The brigade commander, Mr. Vinko Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, you may have heard that a lot of Muslim men, some with guns, like hundreds and hundreds of them were coming out from the Srebrenica enclave and clashed in Baljkovica with the Zvornik Brigade. Do you remember was there any bad feelings among the soldiers, like yourself, towards their commanders that allowed that Muslim column to come running up through the Zvornik area?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice any of that in my unit. In my unit there were no such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you hear about any members in your unit having to go to the cultural centre in Pilica and load hundreds of dead Muslim men in the back of their truck, hauling them up to the Branjevo farm and dropping them there to be buried?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this significantly goes beyond the scope of examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but the rule allows for that contingency as well. So go ahead, please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, sir, I can help you think about that, that this happened on the 17th of July, 1995, and you would have heard about it, if you would have, when you got back from the funeral?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I state with full responsibility that I'm telling you the truth. The members of my R Battalion, into which I was mobilised on the 15th, had nothing to do with Pilica. I claim that in full responsibility. That part of the unit, when I was attending the honour guard on the 16th, was assigned to a road towards Tuzla, that is where they were. No person from that unit was engaged at the location you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Another unit of the R Battalion that did you hear was involved?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I learned of the massacre later on. I didn't know anything about who the executioners were then, nor do I know now who the people were there that did that and whether they were members of the battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Is there re-examination, Ms. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have questions from the Bench either. So Mr. Milosevic, that means that your testimony finishes here. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I would like to thank you very much for having come over to give evidence in this trial and on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back home. Our staff will give you all the assistance you require.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Nikolic, apart from the statement, the 92 ter statement, I suppose there's no document?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No documents were made use of by the Prosecution. So we can move -- proceed with the next witness. My understanding, Ms. Nikolic, is the following, because yesterday of course when you decided, or the day before, when you decided to withdraw (redacted) (redacted) or whatever his name is, I start to think wanting to see whether we were in a position to fill in the time until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the registry informed me that you very diligently managed to provide for another two witnesses to cover the time we would have otherwise had. Is that correct or not? And I take it that the next witness would be Mara Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have two witnesses left for this week, Mara Milosevic and Dusica Sikimic. This would exhaust the number of ten witnesses we called in for this week. I apologise if we'll be forced to have some time left in this week but having in mind the event with the gentleman whose name I don't want to mention, we did our utmost but we are unable to bring any more witnesses this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber certainly cannot criticize you when it comes to diligence. So Mara Milosevic, please. In fact, we can only commend you for your organised way in which you have been conducting your case.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mrs. Milosevic, good afternoon to you. You are most welcome at this Tribunal. You've been summoned as a witness by the Defence team of Drago Nikolic. Before you start your testimony our rules require that you make a solemn declaration that in the course of your evidence you will be speaking the truth. The text is going to be handed to you now, please read it out aloud and that will be your solemn commitment with us. You have to read it out aloud, madam, so that we hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you so much, ma'am. Please make yourself comfortable, sit down. And Ms. Nikolic will be asking you some questions. She will then be followed presumably by Mr. McCloskey for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Milosevic. Do you feel well?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. I feel all right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We've met already but I would kindly ask you to state your first and last name for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My name is Mara Milosevic. I was born in 1950 in Kravica, Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is your current occupation, Mrs. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Are you related to Drago Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are closely related.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Do you recall that you gave a statement to Drago Nikolic's Defence team on the 23rd of April, 2008?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to read this statement at the time when you signed it and also before your testimony when you were being proofed?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In accordance with the 92 ter, I will now read a brief summary of your statement, Mrs. Milosevic. The witness lives in Zvornik. The late Dusan Milosevic is her brother and the Drago Nikolic is her cousin. The witness remembers the events of the 16th and the 17th of July when her brother Dusan Nikolic was killed. He was a military policeman in the Zvornik Brigade. The witness remembers that on the 16th of July, 1995, there were rumours in Zvornik about heavy fighting in Baljkovica and that many soldiers were killed. Dusica, the wife of Dusan Nikolic, and the witness were having coffee together when Dusica said that military police had also sustained losses in Baljkovica. The witness remembers that she called Drago Nikolic at his home and that his wife, Milena, answered the phone and said that Drago had just left and to call him at the command. The witness remembers that she did not call Drago immediately. She felt afraid and together with Slobodanka Gajic she headed towards the Zvornik hospital in the early afternoon. The witness did not want to enter the hospital and remained there at the crossroads and Slobodanka went to ask around what was going on. When Slobodanka came back, she told the witness to call Drago Nikolic to find out what was going on. The witness found this odd, why Slobodanka insisted that she should call Drago Nikolic and she remembers that Slobodanka later explained to her that some people who were in front of the hospital had told her that they had seen Drago Nikolic in hospital and that he was sobbing because a close relative of his had been killed. After she returned from the hospital, the witness made a call to the Zvornik Brigade command and asked Drago Nikolic to tell her about her brother Dusan. Drago told her that he didn't know what was going on and that he would call her back shortly. After awhile, Drago Nikolic did not call the witness but he suddenly showed up in her apartment with her husband Dragan Milosevic and some other people and that is when they told her that Dusan had been killed. There was a nurse with them and she gave first aid to the witness. From that moment on, Drago Nikolic was with his family all the time. He organised the funeral and the transportation of Dusan's body to Dusica's and Dusan's flat on the 17th of July, 1995, in the morning. Dusan's funeral was held in Kravica on the 17th of July, 1995, in the afternoon. The procession with the body with the late Dusan left Zvornik around noon and they took the detours because it was dangerous to go through Konjevic Polje. The witness remembers that Drago Nikolic was with them during all that time, even after Dusan's funeral, and that he helped them a lot, organising everything that was necessary. The witness claims that Dusan's death was a great shock for Drago Nikolic since they had been inseparable from their early childhood. The late Dusan and Drago Nikolic were born in the same year, 1957, they went to school together and they spent time together, they socialised both in Sarajevo and in Zvornik. This completes my 92 ter summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Milosevic, does this summary that I just read to you reflect the statement that you gave to Drago Nikolic's Defence team?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The facts presented in your statement, are they true and accurate?

utterances.speaker: MARA MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
